pr_title: avoid ArgumentOutOfRangeException while processing invalid or incomplete TLS frame
pr_body:
This change fixes issue reported in #62109. The issue has long summary describing what is going on - based on dump provided by the reporter. 

In essence, `FillHandshakeBufferAsync` can "silently fail" on EOF and we can create ArrayBuffer with negative length. Added test would throw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` on release builds or hit `Assert` with debug builds. 

I modified the `FillHandshakeBufferAsync` to consistently throw if EOF is reached before request bytes are accumulated. This was already there in few places but we missed the case when read would finish synchronously. 

fixes #62109

Since we are changing this code anyway:

I don't understand why we have the InternalFillHandshakeBuffferAsync helper here. What is this accomplishing, vs just directly awaiting the task returned by ReadAsync? The async machinery already optimizes for the sync completion case.

I suppose perhaps there is some benefit in avoiding the very small cost of async method setup in the case where we don't need to read at all, but (a) I'm quite skeptical that this cost matters, and (b) even if we want to optimize for it, we can achieve the same result much more easily.

Looking back at the history here, this seems to have happened because we basically copied this code from FillBufferAsync, and that's what FillBufferAsync used to do. But FillBufferAsync was changed to not do this a long time ago.

(Also, FillBufferAsync seems to be not used at all anymore, and should be removed.)

yes, I was thinking about InternalFillHandshakeBuffferAsync, but decided not to change it with this change. It is independent IMHO and would complicate servicing if we would think about it.  It seems like was `FillBufferAsync ` was obsoleted by `EnsureFullTlsFrameAsync`. 
Merging the `_handshakeBuffer` and `_internalBuffer` is on my todo list for a while.
Looks like I open https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/52037 while back for the buffers.

That part will probably not matter. As far as I can tell, this happens before the platform code even executes. 
Here is what I see from one of the dumps:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14356188/147618145-9ccb49da-2ba9-4736-8052-a09992cc9b11.png)

The bytes sequence does not seems to be valid TLS frame. It is either some fuzzer/garbage or Kestrel somehow mangles the data (cc: @Tratcher in case there is some known issue)

Either one should not matter - we should not  get `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.
Since we fail to recognize validation frame, `_framing` will be `Unified` and we hit. 

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/67b110e8b64a101c81f6f8b9746b0648bceb2cf4/src/libraries/System.Net.Security/src/System/Net/Security/SslStream.Implementation.cs#L473-L479

Given sequence of input bytes gives `_lastFrame.Header.Length = 12797` + 5 bytes header is 12802 -> matching the `ActiveStart` above. 

The interesting one is the `AvailableStart` . That basically points to where next bytes should go, suggesting that we got 182 bytes so far. Looking at the actual buffer, there are mostly nonzero bytes in first 182 bytes, followed by all zeros. 

We **_should_** read rest of the frame or fail but we don't seem to
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/67b110e8b64a101c81f6f8b9746b0648bceb2cf4/src/libraries/System.Net.Security/src/System/Net/Security/SslStream.Implementation.cs#L494-L497


and then

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/67b110e8b64a101c81f6f8b9746b0648bceb2cf4/src/libraries/System.Net.Security/src/System/Net/Security/SslStream.Implementation.cs#L560-L567

This updates the `_activeStart`, that makes `ActiveLength` negative and we fail slicing the buffer
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/67b110e8b64a101c81f6f8b9746b0648bceb2cf4/src/libraries/System.Net.Security/src/System/Net/Security/SslStream.Implementation.cs#L594

For some reason `FillHandshakeBufferAsync` does not read the full frame. It may be inconsistent EOF handling between sync/async path but that would not explain why 5.0 would work -> the code is mostly identical.

review_comments:
The general pattern we use for these sorts of "Fill" routines is:

(1) Return 0 if EOF is hit and no data is in the buffer -- i.e. no partial frame is received. This allows the caller to decide if receiving an immediate EOF is an error or not -- it may instead simply indicate graceful shutdown -- and if it is an error, to generate the appropriate exception, since it may be desirable to generate a different exception or message in the EOF case vs the partial frame case.
(2) Throw something like "unexpected EOF" when EOF is hit and there is data in the buffer. This means we received a partial frame, and is always an error.

I believe this is what the calling code expects -- note it checks for 0 bytes on the first call to this, but not on the second, since at that point we must have at least some data in the buffer.

I don't think the presence of data is really relevant here. We call it possibly twice: once with just header size and then with promised frame size. In all cases, we really want to throw IOException if we cannot get enough data to continue. 

We already do that if the read does not finish synchronously here:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/d0631be3a1b9e5a8adf16f4885778179a8ed365b/src/libraries/System.Net.Security/src/System/Net/Security/SslStream.Implementation.cs#L1101
